On examination, she has a low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur heard best at the apex in the left lateral position. Which of the following investigations would be most useful to confirm the diagnosis and assess its severity?
options: {"A":"Cardiac MRI","B":"Chest X-ray","C":"Coronary Angiography","D":"Echocardiography","E":"Electrocardiogram (ECG)"}
feedback: The clinical presentation (history of rheumatic fever, dyspnoea, orthopnoea) and physical examination findings (low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex) are highly suggestive of mitral stenosis. Echocardiography is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing and assessing the severity of valvular heart diseases, including mitral stenosis. It provides detailed information on valve morphology, gradients, and chamber function.

question: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with severe chronic mitral regurgitation secondary to a prolapsed posterior leaflet, causing symptoms of exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. His left ventricular ejection fraction is preserved (60%), and he has no other significant comorbidities. Medical management with ACE inhibitors and diuretics has provided some symptom relief, but he remains symptomatic. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: {"A":"Add a beta-blocker to his current medications","B":"Increase the dose of his current diuretic","C":"Refer for surgical mitral valve repair or replacement","D":"Refer for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)","E":"Recommend regular exercise and watchful waiting"}
feedback: For symptomatic patients with severe primary mitral regurgitation and preserved left ventricular function, surgical mitral valve repair or replacement is generally recommended to relieve symptoms and prevent progression of left ventricular dysfunction. Medical therapies like ACE inhibitors and diuretics can help manage symptoms but do not address the underlying mechanical defect. TAVI is a procedure for aortic valve disease, not mitral. Watchful waiting is not appropriate for symptomatic severe MR.

question:
A 28-year-old male presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of intermittent fever, night sweats, and a persistent cough. He admits to recent intravenous drug use. On examination, his temperature is 38.8°C, heart rate 105 bpm, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. A pansystolic murmur is audible, loudest over the xiphisternum and increasing with inspiration. There are no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. Blood cultures are taken.

Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of infective endocarditis in this patient?
options: {"A":"Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus","B":"Enterococcus faecalis","C":"Staphylococcus aureus","D":"Streptococcus bovis","E":"Viridans group streptococci"}
feedback: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users, often affecting the tricuspid valve (right-sided endocarditis), which aligns with the pansystolic murmur increasing on inspiration. Coagulase-negative Staphylococci are more commonly associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis. Enterococcus faecalis is associated with healthcare-associated infections or genitourinary/gastrointestinal procedures. Streptococcus bovis (now S. gallolyticus) is linked to colorectal pathology. Viridans group streptococci are a common cause of native valve endocarditis, often following dental procedures, but less likely in IVDUs compared to S. aureus.

question:
A 55-year-old man with a history of a bicuspid aortic valve presents to the cardiology clinic with a 3-week history of fatigue, intermittent fever, and a new persistent cough. He denies recent dental procedures. On examination, his temperature is 38.0°C, heart rate 98 bpm, and a new early diastolic murmur is noted at the left sternal edge. His conjunctivae show petechial haemorrhages. Three sets of blood cultures have been sent and are awaiting results.

What is the single most important imaging investigation to further evaluate for infective endocarditis in this patient?
options: {"A":"Cardiac CT scan","B":"Chest X-ray","C":"Myocardial perfusion scan","D":"Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE)","E":"Transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE)"}
feedback: Given the high suspicion of infective endocarditis with a new murmur, fever, and peripheral stigmata in a patient with a predisposing cardiac condition (bicuspid aortic valve), a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) is the most important initial imaging investigation. It allows visualisation of vegetations, assessment of valve damage, and detection of complications. While a transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) is more sensitive, TTE is generally performed first as it is non-invasive and provides valuable information. Cardiac CT and myocardial perfusion scans are not primary diagnostic tools for IE, and a chest X-ray is useful for complications (e.g., septic emboli) but not for direct diagnosis of endocardial lesions.

question:
A 70-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve underwent a dental extraction 4 weeks ago. He presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-week history of worsening fever, malaise, and shortness of breath. On examination, he is febrile (39.2°C), tachycardic (115 bpm), and a new regurgitant murmur is heard over the apex. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Three sets of blood cultures are immediately taken.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial empirical antibiotic regimen for this patient, pending culture results?
options: {"A":"Amoxicillin and Gentamicin","B":"Benzylpenicillin and Gentamicin","C":"Flucloxacillin and Rifampicin","D":"Vancomycin and Gentamicin","E":"Vancomycin and Linezolid"}
feedback: This patient has suspected infective endocarditis on a prosthetic valve. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 1 year of surgery) is commonly caused by Staphylococci (both S. aureus and coagulase-negative Staphylococci, often MRSA) and Gram-negative bacilli. Therefore, empirical treatment must cover these broad possibilities. Vancomycin provides excellent coverage for MRSA and coagulase-negative Staphylococci, while Gentamicin covers Gram-negative organisms and provides synergistic activity against Staphylococci and Enterococci. Amoxicillin/Benzylpenicillin are inappropriate due to likely penicillin resistance in Staphylococci, particularly MRSA. Flucloxacillin is effective against MSSA but not MRSA, and rifampicin is usually added later for synergy once sensitivity is known. Linezolid is an an alternative for MRSA but not typically the first-line empirical choice in combination, and Gentamicin's role is critical for broad-spectrum coverage.

question: You are seeing several patients in your GP clinic. Which of the following patients is at the highest risk of developing infective endocarditis?
options: {"A":"A 45-year-old man with controlled hypertension taking lisinopril.","B":"A 60-year-old woman with well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus.","C":"A 72-year-old man with a history of a previous mitral valve replacement 5 years ago.","D":"A 30-year-old woman with a congenital atrial septal defect (ASD) that was surgically repaired in childhood.","E":"A 50-year-old man with stable angina pectoris managed with nitrates and beta-blockers."}
feedback: Patients with prosthetic heart valves are at a significantly increased risk of developing infective endocarditis throughout their lifetime. While the risk is highest within the first year after surgery, it remains elevated indefinitely compared to the general population. A previous history of endocarditis also confers high risk. Hypertension, well-controlled diabetes, stable angina, and a repaired atrial septal defect (if repaired completely without residual shunting) do not confer the same high risk for IE.

question: A 65-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic complaining of difficulty chewing food and a constant dull ache in his left jaw. On examination, he has weakness of the muscles of mastication on the left side and reduced sensation to light touch over his left cheek and jaw. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
options: {"A":"Facial nerve (VII)","B":"Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)","C":"Hypoglossal nerve (XII)","D":"Trigeminal nerve (V)","E":"Vagus nerve (X)"}
feedback: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) supplies the muscles of mastication (motor) and provides sensation to the face (sensory). Difficulty chewing and reduced sensation in the jaw are characteristic signs of trigeminal nerve pathology.

question: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her family who witnessed her suddenly collapse. On examination, she has expressive aphasia, a dense right-sided hemiparesis (weakness affecting arm and leg), and right-sided hemisensory loss. Her eye gaze is deviated to the left. Which artery is most likely occluded?
options: {"A":"Anterior Cerebral Artery","B":"Basilar Artery","C":"Middle Cerebral Artery","D":"Posterior Cerebral Artery","E":"Vertebral Artery"}
feedback: Expressive aphasia (Broca's area), contralateral hemiparesis, and hemisensory loss (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) with eye deviation towards the side of the lesion (away from the hemiparesis) are classical signs of a stroke affecting the left middle cerebral artery territory.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and numbness in his left leg after a fall two days prior. On examination, he has reduced proprioception and vibration sense in his left leg, along with ipsilateral spasticity. He also reports loss of pain and temperature sensation in his right leg, starting from the mid-thigh downwards. Motor strength in his right leg is normal. Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: {"A":"Right cerebral cortex","B":"Left cerebral cortex","C":"Brainstem","D":"Left hemisection of the spinal cord","E":"Peripheral nerve entrapment at L4-L5"}
feedback: This constellation of symptoms (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/vibration with motor weakness and spasticity, and contralateral loss of pain/temperature) is characteristic of a Brown-Séquard syndrome, which results from hemisection of the spinal cord.

question: A 68-year-old man attends his GP with a 6-month history of developing a resting tremor in his right hand, stiffness in his limbs, and a general slowing of movement. On examination, he has cogwheel rigidity and takes small, shuffling steps. He has no significant sensory deficits. Which of the following brain structures is primarily implicated in the pathology causing his symptoms?
options: {"A":"Cerebellum","B":"Motor Cortex (Precentral Gyrus)","C":"Substantia Nigra (part of the basal ganglia)","D":"Thalamus","E":"Dorsal root ganglia"}
feedback: Resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia are classic symptoms of Parkinson's disease, which is primarily caused by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, a key component of the basal ganglia involved in motor control.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 72-year-old man is brought to the GP by his wife due to concerns about his memory and behaviour over the past year. She reports that his cognitive function fluctuates significantly from day to day, sometimes appearing lucid and at other times very confused. He has started describing seeing "little children playing in the garden" when no one is there, which is distressing for him. She also mentions he frequently acts out his dreams, kicking and shouting during sleep, and has recently developed a tremor in his left hand and a shuffling gait. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Alzheimer's disease","B":"Dementia with Lewy bodies","C":"Fronto-temporal dementia","D":"Vascular dementia","E":"Parkinson's disease dementia"}
feedback: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism. REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams) is also a very common feature, often preceding cognitive decline. Alzheimer's disease typically presents with progressive memory loss as the prominent initial symptom without early prominent hallucinations or parkinsonism. Fronto-temporal dementia primarily presents with early behavioural changes or language difficulties. Vascular dementia often has a stepwise decline and focal neurological signs. Parkinson's disease dementia occurs in patients with established Parkinson's disease, where motor symptoms typically precede the onset of dementia by at least one year; here, the motor symptoms and dementia onset are more concurrent.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: Mrs. Henderson, a 78-year-old woman, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease two years ago and is cared for at home by her daughter, Sarah. Sarah attends a follow-up appointment, expressing increasing exhaustion and stress. She reports that her mother is becoming more agitated in the evenings, frequently wanders, and sometimes resists personal care, leading to arguments. Sarah feels isolated and unsure where to turn for help. Which of the following resources would be most appropriate to suggest as an initial step for Sarah to find practical support?
options: {"A":"Referral for a cholinesterase inhibitor medication review","B":"Contacting her local authority's adult social services department","C":"Arranging for a private live-in carer immediately","D":"Ordering a full neurology consultation and repeat MRI brain scan","E":"Admission to an acute psychiatric ward for assessment"}
feedback: Contacting the local authority's adult social services department is the most appropriate initial step for Sarah. Social services can conduct a needs assessment for both Mrs. Henderson and Sarah, leading to practical support like day care services, respite care, carer support groups, equipment for the home, or advice on managing challenging behaviours. While a medication review might be considered for agitation, it does not address Sarah's immediate need for practical support and respite. Arranging a private live-in carer might be a solution but is often costly and requires a needs assessment first. A full neurology consultation and repeat MRI are generally not indicated for managing existing dementia symptoms and carer burnout. Admission to an acute psychiatric ward is usually reserved for severe behavioural disturbances posing an immediate risk, not the first step for general carer support.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 72-year-old man attends his GP surgery complaining of a sudden onset of left-sided weakness and difficulty speaking which lasted approximately 30 minutes before fully resolving. He has a history of hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes. On examination, his neurological examination is normal. His blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. What is the most appropriate initial diagnosis for this patient's symptoms?
options: {"A":"Ischaemic stroke","B":"Transient ischaemic attack (TIA)","C":"Bell's palsy","D":"Migraine with aura","E":"Hypoglycaemia"}
feedback: The key features are sudden onset, focal neurological deficit (weakness, dysphasia) that fully resolves within 24 hours (in this case 30 minutes). This is the classic definition of a Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA). Ischaemic stroke involves persistent neurological deficit. Bell's palsy typically affects only the facial nerve and would not cause limb weakness or dysphasia. Migraine with aura can cause neurological symptoms, but typically develops over minutes and resolves over hours, often with a headache, and is less common to present with such clear focal motor and speech deficits resolving so quickly without other features. Hypoglycaemia can cause confusion and focal signs but would typically be associated with other systemic symptoms and usually resolves rapidly with glucose. Given the risk factors (hypertension, diabetes), TIA is highly likely and requires urgent investigation.

topic: Teaching Theme – Phase 2a Early Years GP (EYGP) Programme
question: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with sudden onset right-sided weakness and slurred speech, which started 45 minutes ago. She is alert but struggling to move her right arm and leg and her speech is dysarthric. Her medical history includes atrial fibrillation, for which she is on no anticoagulation, and hyperlipidaemia. Her GCS is 15. Her blood pressure is 160/95 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate investigation to determine the management strategy?
options: {"A":"Carotid Doppler ultrasound","B":"Electrocardiogram (ECG)","C":"Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) head scan","D":"Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) head scan","E":"Lumbar puncture"}
feedback: In a patient presenting with acute stroke symptoms, the most crucial immediate investigation is a non-contrast CT head scan to differentiate between ischaemic stroke and haemorrhagic stroke. This distinction is critical because thrombolysis (for ischaemic stroke) is contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke. Carotid Doppler ultrasound and ECG are important investigations for identifying the cause of an ischaemic stroke (e.g., carotid stenosis, atrial fibrillation) but are not the immediate priority for determining acute management. MRI head scan provides more detailed imaging but is often not immediately available in the acute setting and takes longer than CT, which is sufficient to rule out haemorrhage. Lumbar puncture is not indicated in the acute assessment of suspected stroke unless subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected but CT is negative.

question: A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to the Emergency Department after a fall, hitting his head. He is drowsy and complains of a severe headache. A CT head scan shows a large intraparenchymal haemorrhage with significant surrounding oedema causing midline shift. According to the Monro-Kellie hypothesis, which of the following mechanisms initially compensates for the increased intracranial volume in such a situation?
options: {"A":"Increased reabsorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)","B":"Decreased cerebral blood flow","C":"Displacement of intracranial venous blood and CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space","D":"Increased production of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)","E":"Atrophy of brain parenchyma"}
feedback: The Monro-Kellie hypothesis states that the sum of volumes of brain, CSF, and intracranial blood is constant. An increase in one component must be offset by a decrease in another. In the acute setting of a space-occupying lesion or oedema, the initial compensatory mechanisms include displacement of intracranial venous blood and CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space. Increased CSF reabsorption or decreased cerebral blood flow are not the primary *initial* compensatory mechanisms described by the hypothesis in this context. Increased CSF production would worsen ICP. Brain atrophy is a chronic process, not an acute compensatory mechanism.

question: A 28-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the Emergency Department after a high-speed collision. He was initially conscious and talking at the scene but became increasingly confused over the past hour. On examination, his GCS is E3V4M6 and his right pupil is dilated and sluggish to react. A CT head scan is urgently performed. Which of the following findings would be most characteristic of an acute extradural haematoma?
options: {"A":"A crescent-shaped collection of blood conforming to the brain surface","B":"A lens-shaped (biconvex) collection of blood not crossing suture lines","C":"A diffuse collection of blood in the subarachnoid space","D":"Multiple petechial haemorrhages within the brain parenchyma","E":"A fluid collection with air-fluid levels in the subdural space"}
feedback: An extradural (epidural) haematoma is typically caused by a laceration of the middle meningeal artery, often associated with a skull fracture. The arterial bleeding collects between the dura and the inner table of the skull, creating a characteristic lens-shaped (biconvex) appearance on CT that does not cross suture lines because the dura is tightly attached at the sutures. A crescent-shaped collection is characteristic of a subdural haematoma, which crosses suture lines but is limited by the falx and tentorium. Diffuse subarachnoid blood indicates subarachnoid haemorrhage. Petechial haemorrhages are seen in diffuse axonal injury or hemorrhagic contusions. Air-fluid levels would suggest a complication like infection or communication with sinuses.

question: A 6-month-old infant with a known history of hydrocephalus managed with a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is brought to the clinic by her parents. They report she has been more irritable than usual, has had intermittent vomiting, and her anterior fontanelle appears more tense and bulging than before. On examination, the shunt site over her skull is tender. What is the most appropriate initial investigation in this suspected case of shunt malfunction?
options: {"A":"Lumbar puncture","B":"MRI brain and full spine","C":"Plain X-rays of the shunt pathway (shunt series)","D":"CT head scan","E":"Electroencephalogram (EEG)"}
feedback: The symptoms (irritability, vomiting, bulging fontanelle) in an infant with a VP shunt are highly suggestive of shunt malfunction, most commonly due to obstruction, infection, or disconnection, leading to re-accumulation of CSF and raised intracranial pressure. A CT head scan is the most appropriate initial investigation to assess ventricular size, look for evidence of obstruction, and rule out other intracranial pathology. A shunt series (X-rays) can check for mechanical integrity (disconnection, fracture) of the shunt tubing but does not assess ventricular size or ICP directly. MRI is more detailed but takes longer and often requires sedation in infants; CT is faster for acute assessment of ventricular size. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in raised ICP with communicating hydrocephalus due to shunt malfunction as it can precipitate herniation. EEG is for seizure activity and not primarily for shunt malfunction.

question: A 48-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of the 'worst headache of his life', which started suddenly while he was lifting weights at the gym. He describes it as a thunderclap headache, associated with neck stiffness and photophobia. On examination, he is conscious but distressed, and his Glasgow Coma Scale is 15. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate *initial* diagnostic investigation for this patient?
options: {"A":"Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) of the brain","B":"CT head scan without contrast","C":"Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia","D":"Cerebral angiography","E":"Carotid Doppler ultrasound"}
feedback: The presentation of a sudden onset 'thunderclap' headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia is highly suspicious for a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), often due to a ruptured intracranial aneurysm. The most appropriate *initial* diagnostic investigation is an urgent CT head scan without contrast. This can detect SAH with high sensitivity, especially within the first 6-12 hours. If the CT scan is negative but clinical suspicion remains high (e.g., beyond the acute phase where blood may no longer be visible on CT), a lumbar puncture to check for xanthochromia (yellow discoloration of CSF due to bilirubin breakdown products from red blood cells) would be the next step. MRA or cerebral angiography are used to identify the source of bleeding (e.g., aneurysm) *after* SAH is diagnosed, not as the initial diagnostic test for SAH itself. Carotid Doppler ultrasound is for carotid artery disease.

question: A 68-year-old man presents to his GP with a 4-week history of worsening headaches and recent onset of confusion. He has a significant smoking history and was treated for a 'chest infection' three months ago that did not fully resolve. Imaging reveals multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction. Regarding the epidemiology of brain tumours in adults, which of the following statements is most accurate?
options: {"A":"Primary brain tumours are more common than metastatic brain tumours","B":"Meningiomas are the most common malignant primary brain tumour","C":"Metastatic brain tumours are more common than primary brain tumours","D":"Glioblastomas are the most common brain tumour in the paediatric population","E":"Brain tumours account for 15% of all new cancer diagnoses in the UK annually"}
feedback: C is correct because in the adult population, metastatic (secondary) brain tumours are significantly more common than primary brain tumours. Common primary sites include the lung, breast, and kidney. A is incorrect as it reverses this relationship. B is incorrect because while meningiomas are common, they are usually benign. D is incorrect because glioblastomas are primarily adult tumours; medulloblastomas and pilocytic astrocytomas are more common in children. E is incorrect as brain tumours are relatively rare compared to other cancers, accounting for roughly 2-3% of all new cancer cases.

question: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her husband. Over the past two months, she has become increasingly apathetic and has started making inappropriate social comments. She complains of a dull, generalized headache that is most severe when she wakes up in the morning and is occasionally associated with vomiting. On examination, she has bilateral papilloedema. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
options: {"A":"Cerebellum","B":"Frontal lobe","C":"Occipital lobe","D":"Parietal lobe","E":"Temporal lobe"}
feedback: B is correct. The patient's personality changes (apathy, social disinhibition) are classic 'frontal lobe signs'. The morning headache and papilloedema indicate raised intracranial pressure (ICP). A is incorrect as cerebellar lesions typically present with ataxia and nystagmus. C is incorrect as occipital lesions cause visual field defects (e.g., homonymous hemianopia). D is incorrect as parietal lesions often cause sensory loss or neglect. E is incorrect as temporal lesions may cause receptive aphasia or complex partial seizures.

question: A 55-year-old man undergoes a debulking procedure for a rapidly progressing high-grade glioma in the right cerebral hemisphere. Histopathological examination of the specimen shows high cellularity, pleomorphic cells, prominent vascular endothelial proliferation, and areas of necrosis surrounded by rows of neoplastic cells. What is the characteristic pathological term for this specific pattern of necrosis?
options: {"A":"Caseating necrosis","B":"Fibrinoid necrosis","C":"Liquefactive necrosis","D":"Pseudopalisading necrosis","E":"Schiller-Duval bodies"}
feedback: D is correct. Pseudopalisading necrosis is a hallmark histological feature of Glioblastoma (WHO Grade 4). It refers to the arrangement of tumour cells around central areas of necrosis. A is incorrect as caseating necrosis is typical of tuberculosis. B is incorrect as fibrinoid necrosis is seen in vasculitis. C is incorrect as it is the general type of necrosis seen in CNS tissue, but 'pseudopalisading' is the specific diagnostic term for this tumour pattern. E is incorrect as Schiller-Duval bodies are found in yolk sac tumours.

question: A 45-year-old man presents to the hospital with his first generalized tonic-clonic seizure. A CT head reveals a single 3cm hypodense lesion in the left temporal lobe with significant surrounding vasogenic oedema and a 5mm shift of the midline structures. While waiting for neurosurgical review and definitive diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management to reduce the vasogenic oedema?
options: {"A":"Acetazolamide","B":"Dexamethasone","C":"Furosemide","D":"Mannitol","E":"Phenytoin"}
feedback: B is correct. High-dose corticosteroids, typically dexamethasone, are the gold standard for reducing vasogenic oedema associated with brain tumours. This reduces the mass effect and improves symptoms. A and C are incorrect as they are diuretics that do not effectively treat cerebral vasogenic oedema. D is incorrect as mannitol is used for the acute, short-term reduction of severely raised ICP (e.g., brain herniation) rather than managing tumour-related oedema. E is incorrect because while phenytoin may be used to prevent further seizures, it does not treat the underlying oedema or mass effect.

question: A 45-year-old man who suffered a traumatic brain injury six months ago is being reviewed in the neuro-rehabilitation clinic. He has residual right-sided hemiparesis which prevents him from walking unaided. Because he cannot walk independently, he has been unable to return to his previous occupation as a delivery driver. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), the patient's inability to return to his job is best classified as which of the following?
options: {"A":"Activity limitation","B":"Environmental factor","C":"Impairment","D":"Participation restriction","S":"Personal factor"}
feedback: The WHO ICF model classifies functioning into three levels: Impairment (problems in body function or structure, e.g., hemiparesis), Activity limitation (difficulties in executing a task, e.g., inability to walk), and Participation restriction (problems in involvement in life situations, e.g., inability to work/return to a job). Environmental and Personal factors are contextual factors that influence the impact of the condition.

question: A 34-year-old woman with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis is reviewed by her GP. She reports that her legs feel increasingly stiff, making it difficult to transfer from her bed to her wheelchair. She also experiences painful involuntary muscle spasms at night. On examination, there is increased resistance to passive movement in both lower limbs, which is velocity-dependent. There is no evidence of a urinary tract infection. What is the most appropriate first-line oral pharmacological treatment for this patient's spasticity?
options: {"A":"Baclofen","B":"Botulinum toxin type A","C":"Dantrolene","D":"Intrathecal baclofen","E":"Tizanidine"}
feedback: Baclofen (a GABA-B agonist) or Gabapentin are generally recommended as first-line oral treatments for generalized spasticity in multiple sclerosis in the UK (NICE guidelines). Tizanidine and Dantrolene are typically used as second-line oral options. Botulinum toxin is used for focal spasticity rather than generalized stiffness, and intrathecal baclofen is reserved for severe, refractory spasticity.

question: An 82-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease is seen at home by a member of the multi-disciplinary team. He describes frequent episodes where his feet feel 'glued to the floor' when trying to walk through narrow doorways or when turning to sit down. This 'freezing of gait' has recently led to several near-miss falls. Which of the following neuro-rehabilitation interventions is most likely to help the patient overcome these specific freezing episodes?
options: {"A":"Ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs)","B":"Occupational therapy for home adaptations like grab rails","C":"Physiotherapy for visual and auditory cueing strategies","D":"Social work assessment for a residential care placement","E":"Speech and language therapy for swallowing assessment"}
feedback: Freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease is often managed using cueing strategies, taught by a physiotherapist. These involve using external stimuli (e.g., stepping over a laser line or walking to the beat of a metronome) to bypass the dysfunctional basal ganglia loops. While home adaptations (OT) improve safety, they do not specifically treat the FOG mechanism itself.

question: A 17-year-old male with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy is attending a specialist clinic to discuss his move from paediatric to adult neurology services. He has complex medical needs, including a gastrostomy for nutrition and controlled epilepsy. Which statement best reflects the core principle of 'transition' as defined in UK clinical practice?
options: {"A":"A single point-in-time event where care is transferred on the 18th birthday","B":"The automatic discharge from specialist therapy services upon leaving school","C":"The legal requirement to transfer all decision-making to the patient at age 16","D":"A planned, purposeful process addressing medical, psychosocial, and vocational needs","E":"The relocation of care to a primary care-led model without specialist input"}
feedback: Transition is defined as the 'purposeful, planned process that addresses the medical, psychosocial and educational/vocational needs of adolescents and young adults with chronic physical and medical conditions as they move from child-centred to adult-oriented health care systems.' It is distinct from 'transfer,' which is the actual point-in-time move of clinical responsibility.

subtopic: Consciousness: its assessment and common disorders
question: A 19-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedics following a fall from a height of 4 metres. On arrival, he opens his eyes only when the clinician applies pressure to his supraorbital notch. He is making incomprehensible groaning sounds but no recognisable words. When his fingernail bed is squeezed, he pulls his hand away from the stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
feedback: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is calculated based on Eye (E), Verbal (V), and Motor (M) responses. This patient scores E2 (opens eyes to pressure), V2 (incomprehensible sounds), and M4 (normal flexion/withdrawal from pain), giving a total score of 8. A score of 8 or less is generally used to define a state of coma and indicates that the patient may be unable to maintain their own airway.

subtopic: Consciousness: its assessment and common disorders
question: A 22-year-old university student presents to the neurology clinic complaining of severe daytime sleepiness that interferes with her lectures. She reports that on several occasions, when she has been laughing with friends, her knees have suddenly buckled, causing her to fall to the floor. During these episodes, she remains fully aware of her surroundings but is unable to move for several seconds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Absence seizures","B":"Cataplexy","C":"Narcolepsy type 1","D":"Orthostatic hypotension","E":"Vasovagal syncope"}
feedback: Narcolepsy type 1 is characterised by the pentad of excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, and disrupted nocturnal sleep. Cataplexy (option B) is the sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions (like laughter) while maintaining consciousness; however, it is a symptom of the underlying disorder, Narcolepsy type 1. Absence seizures involve a loss of awareness. Syncope involves a loss of consciousness.

subtopic: Consciousness: its assessment and common disorders
question: A 55-year-old woman remains on a neurorehabilitation ward six weeks after suffering a severe hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury following a cardiac arrest. She has regular periods where her eyes are open and she appears to follow a sleep-wake cycle. However, despite extensive testing, she shows no evidence of purposeful response to visual, auditory, or tactile stimuli, and there is no evidence of language comprehension. In the context of the medical definition of consciousness, how is this state best described?
options: {"A":"High wakefulness with high awareness","B":"High wakefulness with low awareness","C":"Low wakefulness with high awareness","D":"Low wakefulness with low awareness","E":"Fluctuating wakefulness with high awareness"}
feedback: Consciousness is clinically divided into two components: wakefulness (arousal/eyes open) and awareness (content of consciousness/purposeful interaction). A vegetative state (or Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome) is characterised by the presence of wakefulness (sleep-wake cycles, eyes opening) but an absence of awareness. High wakefulness with high awareness describes normal consciousness; low wakefulness and low awareness describes coma or deep anaesthesia.

subtopic: Consciousness: its assessment and common disorders
question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department after being found collapsed in the street. On examination, he does not open his eyes to pressure, makes no vocal sounds, and shows an extensor response to painful stimuli. His blood glucose is 5.4 mmol/L [3.9-5.8 mmol/L] and his oxygen saturations are 94% on room air. What is the most immediate management priority for this patient?
options: {"A":"Arrange an urgent CT head","B":"Intravenous fluid resuscitation","C":"Intravenous thiamine administration","D":"Maintenance of a patent airway","E":"Perform a lumbar puncture"}
feedback: The patient has a GCS of 4 (E1, V1, M2). In clinical practice, impairment of consciousness is a critical sign of physiological instability. The mantra 'GCS 8 or less, intubate' reflects the fact that patients with a significantly reduced level of consciousness lose their protective airway reflexes (swallowing/coughing) and are at high risk of airway obstruction or aspiration. Airway (A) must be secured before moving to further investigations like CT (D) or lumbar puncture (E).

question: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the stroke unit with sudden onset incoordination. On examination, he has left-sided limb ataxia, dysmetria, and an intention tremor. He also demonstrates a left-sided Horner's syndrome and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of his face, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature on his right side. An MRI confirms a lateral medullary infarct. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be occluded?
options: {"A":"Anterior inferior cerebellar artery","B":"Basilar artery","C":"Middle cerebral artery","D":"Posterior inferior cerebellar artery","E":"Superior cerebellar artery"}
feedback: The clinical presentation describes Wallenberg’s syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome). This is most commonly caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). The cerebellar signs (ipsilateral limb ataxia) result from damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Other features include ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral facial sensory loss, and contralateral body sensory loss. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome, which typically includes ipsilateral facial nerve paralysis and deafness.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a three-month history of progressive walking difficulties. On examination, the neurologist notes that her speech is slow, slurred, and has an irregular rhythm, often referred to as 'scanning speech'. When asked to perform a rapid alternating movement task (such as 'clapping' one hand on the other, alternating palm and back of the hand), she is unable to maintain a regular rhythm. What is the correct medical term for this specific finding?
options: {"A":"Dysdiadochokinesia","B":"Dysmetria","C":"Hypokinesia","D":"Rebound phenomenon","E":"Titubation"}
feedback: Dysdiadochokinesia is the medical term for the inability to perform rapid alternating movements, a classic sign of cerebellar dysfunction. Dysmetria refers to the 'past-pointing' or lack of coordination in distance/range of movement. Titubation refers to a rhythmic tremor of the head or trunk. Scanning speech and dysdiadochokinesia are part of the 'DANISH' mnemonic for cerebellar signs (Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Slurred/Scanning speech, Hypotonia).

question: A 19-year-old man presents to his GP with a one-year history of worsening balance and frequent stumbling. On examination, he is noted to have significant gait ataxia and a high-arched foot deformity (pes cavus). Neurological examination reveals absent ankle and knee jerk reflexes, and his plantar responses are extensor. His older sister was recently diagnosed with a similar condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Ataxia-telangiectasia","B":"Cerebellar hypoplasia","C":"Friedreich’s ataxia","D":"Multiple sclerosis","E":"Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1"}
feedback: Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder (GAA) that typically presents in the second decade of life. Key clinical features include progressive gait and limb ataxia, pes cavus, kyphoscoliosis, and the characteristically 'mixed' neurological picture of absent lower limb reflexes (due to peripheral neuropathy) and extensor plantar responses (due to upper motor neuron involvement in the corticospinal tracts). Multiple sclerosis usually presents with relapsing-remitting episodes and is less likely to have pes cavus.

question: A 52-year-old man with a long-term history of heavy alcohol consumption is brought to the Emergency Department by his partner. She is concerned because he has become increasingly confused over the last 48 hours and is unable to walk steadily. On examination, the patient has a broad-based, staggering gait and shows significant truncal instability. On cranial nerve examination, there is a paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle on both sides. What is the immediate pathophysiological cause of these symptoms?
options: {"A":"Autoimmune destruction of Purkinje cells","B":"Cerebellar cortical atrophy due to direct ethanol toxicity","C":"Demyelination of the vestibular nerve","D":"Ischaemia of the vermis","E":"Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency"}
feedback: The triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia (such as lateral rectus palsy/abducens nerve palsy) in the context of alcohol excess is diagnostic of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. This is caused by a deficiency in thiamine (Vitamin B1), which acts as a co-factor for several key enzymes in glucose metabolism. While chronic alcohol use can lead to permanent cerebellar cortical atrophy (specifically affecting the superior vermis), the acute presentation of the classic triad necessitates immediate treatment with thiamine to prevent progression to Korsakoff’s syndrome.

question: A 32-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Which of the following best describes the primary pathological process occurring in the central nervous system in this condition?
options: {"A":"Accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles","B":"Demyelination and axonal damage","C":"Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra","D":"Formation of Lewy bodies in cortical and subcortical regions","E":"Autoimmune destruction of acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction"}
feedback: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by immune-mediated demyelination and subsequent axonal damage within the central nervous system. Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are seen in Alzheimer's disease. Loss of dopaminergic neurons is characteristic of Parkinson's disease. Lewy bodies are associated with Parkinson's and Lewy body dementia. Autoimmune destruction of acetylcholine receptors occurs in myasthenia gravis.

question: A 28-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with a 3-week history of blurred vision in his right eye, described as a "greying out" of colour vision, associated with pain on eye movement. He also reports an episode 6 months ago of transient numbness and tingling in his left arm and leg which resolved spontaneously. On examination, he has reduced visual acuity in the right eye and an afferent pupillary defect. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
options: {"A":"Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis","B":"Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the brain and spinal cord","C":"Visual evoked potentials (VEPs)","D":"Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS)","E":"Serum anti-aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibody test"}
feedback: The patient's presentation with optic neuritis (blurred vision, pain on eye movement, afferent pupillary defect) and a history of previous neurological symptoms (numbness/tingling) disseminated in time and space, is highly suggestive of multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain and spinal cord is the most crucial investigation to demonstrate characteristic demyelinating lesions, which are often disseminated in space. While CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands) and VEPs (demonstrating slowed conduction) can support the diagnosis, MRI is typically the primary diagnostic tool. EMG/NCS are for peripheral nerve disorders. AQP4 antibodies are for Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD).

question: A 35-year-old woman has recently been diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS). She asks her GP about disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) to reduce the frequency and severity of her relapses. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action for most currently approved DMTs in RRMS?
options: {"A":"Direct repair of damaged myelin","B":"Suppression or modulation of the immune system","C":"Enhancement of neuronal conduction","D":"Prevention of neuronal excitotoxicity","E":"Promotion of axonal regeneration"}
feedback: Most disease-modifying therapies for relapsing-remitting MS work by suppressing or modulating the immune system to reduce the inflammatory attacks on the myelin and axons in the CNS. While research is ongoing for myelin repair and axonal regeneration, these are not the primary mechanisms of currently approved DMTs. Enhancing neuronal conduction or preventing excitotoxicity are not the main mechanisms of action for existing DMTs in MS.

question: A 45-year-old man has been living with multiple sclerosis for 15 years. Initially, he experienced distinct relapses followed by periods of full recovery. Over the past 5 years, his neurological function has been steadily worsening with increasing spasticity and gait difficulties, without clear relapses or remissions. What is the most appropriate classification for his current disease course?
options: {"A":"Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS)","B":"Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)","C":"Secondary Progressive MS (SPMS)","D":"Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS)","E":"Benign MS"}
feedback: The patient's history describes an initial phase of relapses and remissions, followed by a gradual, steady worsening of neurological function without distinct relapses. This is characteristic of Secondary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (SPMS). Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS) involves distinct relapses and remissions. Primary Progressive MS (PPMS) involves a steady decline from the outset, without initial relapses. Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS) is the first clinical episode suggestive of MS. Benign MS is a retrospective diagnosis where, after 15 years, a patient has minimal disability.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP complaining of severe headaches for the past 6 months. These headaches typically occur 2-3 times a month, last for up to 48 hours, and are described as throbbing and unilateral, often affecting the right side of her head. During an attack, she experiences extreme sensitivity to light and sound, and feels nauseous, sometimes vomiting. She finds lying in a dark, quiet room provides some relief. She has tried over-the-counter painkillers with limited success. Neurological examination is unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Cluster headache","B":"Glaucoma","C":"Migraine with aura","D":"Migraine without aura","E":"Tension-type headache"}
feedback: The patient's symptoms (unilateral, throbbing pain, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea/vomiting, lasting up to 48 hours, periodicity) are classic for migraine. There is no mention of a preceding aura, making migraine without aura the most likely specific diagnosis. Cluster headache typically presents with severe unilateral pain, often orbital/temporal, with associated autonomic features (e.g., lacrimation, ptosis) and shorter duration. Tension headache is usually bilateral, dull, non-pulsating, and not associated with severe photophobia/phonophobia or nausea. Glaucoma would typically have eye pain and visual disturbance.

question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden-onset, "worst headache of his life" that began while he was exercising. He describes it as an explosive pain across the back of his head and neck. On examination, he is alert but distressed, with neck stiffness and photophobia. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 15. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his head, performed within 6 hours of symptom onset, appears normal.
What is the most appropriate next step in the investigation?
options: {"A":"Discharge home with analgesia and safety netting advice","B":"Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain","C":"Lumbar puncture","D":"Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)","E":"Repeat CT scan in 24 hours"}
feedback: The patient's "thunderclap headache" description, sudden onset, and associated meningism are highly suspicious for a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), even with a normal CT scan performed within 6 hours. While a CT within 6 hours has high sensitivity for SAH, it is not 100%. A lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia (breakdown products of red blood cells) is the gold standard investigation to definitively rule out SAH when the CT is negative but clinical suspicion remains high. MRI is not typically used for acute SAH diagnosis. MRA might be considered later to look for an aneurysm if SAH is confirmed. Repeating a CT scan might delay diagnosis and is less sensitive than LP for detecting SAH after a negative initial CT.

question: Which of the following neurotransmitters is thought to play a central role in the pathophysiology of migraine attacks, particularly in the activation of the trigeminal pain pathway?
options: {"A":"Acetylcholine","B":"Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)","C":"Dopamine","D":"Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)","E":"Serotonin (5-HT)"}
feedback: Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a key neuropeptide involved in migraine pathophysiology. It is released from trigeminal nerve endings and is a potent vasodilator, contributing to neurogenic inflammation and pain signalling in the trigeminal system. Antibodies targeting CGRP or its receptor are now a significant class of migraine prophylactic medications. While serotonin (5-HT) also plays a role, particularly in older theories and the mechanism of triptans, CGRP is considered more central to the acute pain pathway activation in current understanding. Acetylcholine, dopamine, and GABA have roles in other neurological functions but are not considered primary mediators of migraine pain in this specific context.

question:
A 40-year-old man presents with a history of recurrent, excruciatingly severe headaches occurring multiple times a day for the past two weeks. The pain is always unilateral, orbital, and described as a "stabbing hot poker" behind his left eye. During attacks, which last about 45 minutes, his left eye waters, his left nostril becomes blocked, and he develops a mild ptosis on the left side. He paces restlessly during the attacks. Neurological examination is normal between attacks.
What is the most appropriate acute abortive treatment for this patient's headaches?
options: {"A":"Oral sumatriptan","B":"Intravenous opioids","C":"High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask","D":"Oral ibuprofen","E":"Propranolol"}
feedback: The clinical picture of severe, unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, nasal congestion, ptosis) and restlessness, lasting about 45 minutes and occurring in bouts, is classic for cluster headache. High-flow oxygen (100% oxygen at 12-15 L/min for 15-20 minutes) is a highly effective acute abortive treatment for cluster headaches. Subcutaneous sumatriptan is also effective, but oral sumatriptan has a slower onset and is less effective for the rapid onset and short duration of cluster attacks. Opioids are generally discouraged due to lack of efficacy and risk of dependence. NSAIDs like ibuprofen are generally ineffective for cluster headache pain. Propranolol is a prophylactic treatment for other headache types, not an acute abortive treatment for cluster headache.

question: A 22 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after collapsing while standing in a crowded queue at a concert. Witnesses describe him becoming pale and sweaty before falling. He was unconscious for approximately 30 seconds, during which he had three brief 'jerking' movements of his arms. He recovered consciousness quickly and was fully oriented within one minute. On arrival, his observations are: Heart rate 72 bpm, Blood pressure 124/80 mmHg, and random plasma glucose 5.1 mmol/L (4.0 - 6.0 mmol/L). What is the most likely cause of his collapse?
options: {"A":"Cardiac arrhythmia","B":"Generalized tonic-clonic seizure","C":"Hypoglycaemic episode","D":"Orthostatic hypotension","E":"Vasovagal syncope"}
feedback: E is correct because the clinical picture (prodromal sweating/pallor, trigger of prolonged standing in a crowd, and rapid recovery) is classic for vasovagal syncope. Brief myoclonic jerks ('convulsive syncope') are common in syncope and do not necessarily indicate epilepsy. A is less likely given the prodrome and clear trigger. B is incorrect as post-ictal confusion is usually prolonged and the jerking in syncope is typically brief and non-rhythmic. C is excluded by the normal glucose.

question: A 19 year old woman is diagnosed with Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) after experiencing several generalized tonic-clonic seizures and frequent early-morning 'jerks' that cause her to drop objects. She is otherwise healthy and is sexually active. According to current UK guidelines (NICE/MHRA), which medication is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient?
options: {"A":"Carbamazepine","B":"Ethosuximide","C":"Levetiracetam","D":"Phenytoin","E":"Sodium Valproate"}
feedback: C is correct. While Sodium Valproate is highly effective for JME, it is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place due to its high teratogenic risk. Levetiracetam is the preferred first-line alternative for generalized seizures in this demographic. Carbamazepine (A) and Phenytoin (D) can actually exacerbate myoclonic seizures. Ethosuximide (B) is used for absence seizures but not for tonic-clonic or myoclonic seizures.

question: A 45 year old man with focal epilepsy is prescribed carbamazepine to manage his seizures. What is the primary mechanism of action of this medication?
options: {"A":"Antagonism of NMDA glutamate receptors","B":"Binding to the synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A)","C":"Inhibition of T-type calcium channels","D":"Potentiation of GABA-A receptor-mediated chloride currents","E":"Use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels"}
feedback: E is correct. Carbamazepine works by stabilizing the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels, making neurons less excitable. A describes the mechanism of drugs like perampanel or ketamine. B is the mechanism of levetiracetam. C is the mechanism of ethosuximide. D describes the mechanism of benzodiazepines and barbiturates.

question: A 30 year old woman is seen in the neurology clinic. She describes episodes that begin with an unusual 'metallic taste' in her mouth and a rising sensation in her stomach. Her partner notes that during these episodes, she stops talking, stares blankly, and repeatedly picks at her buttons for about two minutes. She has no memory of the events. Which type of seizure is most likely being described?
options: {"A":"Absence seizure","B":"Atonic seizure","C":"Focal impaired awareness seizure","D":"Myoclonic seizure","E":"Tonic seizure"}
feedback: C is correct. The description of an 'aura' (metallic taste, epigastric rising) followed by automatisms (picking at clothes) and impaired consciousness is characteristic of a focal impaired awareness seizure, typically arising from the temporal lobe. Absence seizures (A) are much shorter (seconds), lack a preceding aura, and do not typically feature complex automatisms. Atonic (B), myoclonic (D), and tonic (E) seizures are generalized seizure types with distinct motor characteristics and no aura.

question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with weakness in her right leg that has persisted for three weeks. On examination, when she attempts to flex her right hip against resistance while lying supine, the weakness is profound. However, when the clinician asks her to flex her left hip against resistance, the clinician feels the right heel involuntarily press down (extend) into their hand with significant force. What is the name of this clinical sign?
options: {"A":"Babinski sign","B":"Gowers' sign","C":"Hoover's sign","D":"Romberg's test","E":"Trendelenburg sign"}
feedback: Hoover's sign is a classic clinical test used to diagnose functional leg weakness. It relies on the principle of 'synergistic contraction'. In a patient with functional weakness, voluntary hip flexion in the 'good' leg leads to involuntary hip extension in the 'weak' leg. A positive Hoover's sign (finding strength in the weak leg during contralateral movement) is highly specific for FND.

question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a suspected seizure. His partner describes the event as lasting approximately 10 minutes. During the episode, his eyes were tightly closed, his head moved rhythmically from side-to-side, and there was evidence of pelvic thrusting. He did not bite his tongue or lose continence. He was tearful and communicative within three minutes of the movements stopping. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Absence seizure","B":"Frontal lobe epilepsy","C":"Functional (dissociative) seizures","D":"Generalized tonic-clonic seizure","E":"Vasovagal syncope"}
feedback: Functional seizures (also known as dissociative seizures) often present with features that distinguish them from epileptic seizures, including a longer duration (>2 minutes), closed eyes (epileptic seizures usually involve open eyes), side-to-side head movements, and pelvic thrusting. Rapid recovery of orientation and emotionality (tearfulness) post-event are also common indicators of FND rather than epilepsy.

question: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with a functional movement disorder after a thorough assessment. He expresses relief that his MRI and EMG results are normal but is confused as to how he can have symptoms without a 'lesion'. According to current evidence-based management concepts for FND, what is the most appropriate first-line intervention?
options: {"A":"Admission for inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation","B":"Commencement of high-dose SSRI therapy","C":"Long-term referral for psychoanalysis","D":"Providing a clear and transparent explanation of the diagnosis","E":"Reassurance that the symptoms are 'all in his head' and will resolve spontaneously"}
feedback: The most important first step in the management of FND is providing a clear, transparent, and non-judgmental explanation. This involves explaining that the 'hardware' (the structure of the brain) is normal, but the 'software' (how the brain sends and receives signals) is malfunctioning. Patients who understand and accept the diagnosis have significantly better outcomes and are more likely to engage with subsequent therapies like specialized physiotherapy or CBT.

question: Recent neurobiological models of Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) emphasize the role of 'predictive coding' and altered brain connectivity. In this context, which of the following is proposed as a core mechanism underlying the development of functional symptoms?
options: {"A":"Abnormal top-down expectations and excessive self-focused attention","B":"Autoimmune-mediated destruction of myelin in the motor cortex","C":"Intentional fabrication of symptoms to achieve a specific secondary gain","D":"Irreversible neurodegeneration of the dopaminergic pathways","E":"Localized ischaemia within the internal capsule"}
feedback: Modern neurobiological theories of FND suggest it is a disorder of 'predictive coding'. It is proposed that the brain generates an abnormal 'prior' or expectation of a symptom (like weakness or a tremor). When coupled with excessive attention directed toward the body part, this 'top-down' signal overrides 'bottom-up' sensory input, resulting in the experience of a physical symptom despite normal underlying structures. It is distinct from malingering (option C), which is the intentional faking of symptoms.

question: A 62-year-old man dies following a three-year history of progressive limb weakness and respiratory failure. Post-mortem examination of the spinal cord reveals degeneration of the corticospinal tracts and significant loss of anterior horn cells. Histopathological staining of the remaining motor neurons identifies ubiquitinated protein inclusions. Which protein is the most likely primary component of these inclusions in this patient?
options: {"A":"Alpha-synuclein","B":"Beta-amyloid","C":"Huntingtin","D":"Tau protein","E":"TDP-43"}
feedback: TDP-43 (transactive response DNA-binding protein 43) is the pathological hallmark of Motor Neurone Disease (MND), found in approximately 97% of cases. It is normally found in the nucleus but mislocalizes to the cytoplasm where it forms aggregates. Alpha-synuclein is associated with Parkinson’s disease and Multiple System Atrophy; Beta-amyloid and Tau are associated with Alzheimer's disease; Huntingtin is the protein associated with Huntington's disease.

question: A 68-year-old woman presents to her GP with a six-month history of progressive difficulty with fine motor tasks, such as doing up buttons. On examination, there is noticeable wasting of the first dorsal interosseous muscle on the right hand with visible fasciculations. However, the biceps and triceps reflexes are remarkably brisk (3+) on the same arm, and the right plantar response is extensor. Sensory examination is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis","B":"Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy","C":"Guillain-Barré Syndrome","D":"Multiple Sclerosis","E":"Myasthenia Gravis"}
feedback: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the coexistence of upper motor neurone (UMN) signs (brisk reflexes, extensor plantar) and lower motor neurone (LMN) signs (wasting, fasciculations) in the same territory, without sensory loss. Cervical spondylosis can cause mixed signs but usually involves sensory changes or bladder dysfunction. Guillain-Barré is primarily a LMN/peripheral nerve disorder. Multiple Sclerosis is a UMN disorder and usually has sensory involvement. Myasthenia Gravis affects the neuromuscular junction and does not cause UMN signs or fasciculations.

question: A 71-year-old man is diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease in a specialist clinic. He is experiencing significant spasticity in his legs and is concerned about his survival time. Which of the following pharmacological interventions is currently the only treatment licensed in the UK to prolong life in patients with this condition?
options: {"A":"Baclofen","B":"Edaravone","C":"Gabapentin","D":"Pyridostigmine","E":"Riluzole"}
feedback: Riluzole is a glutamate antagonist and is currently the only drug recommended by NICE in the UK to extend survival (typically by 2-3 months) in patients with MND. Baclofen is used for symptomatic relief of spasticity but does not alter disease progression. Edaravone is used in some countries but is not currently standard UK practice. Pyridostigmine is used for Myasthenia Gravis. Gabapentin may be used for neuropathic pain or cramps but has no effect on survival.

question: A 65-year-old patient is recently diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease. The neurologist explains the typical progression of the disease and discusses advance care planning. Which of the following clinical features at the time of presentation is most strongly associated with a poorer prognosis and shorter median survival time?
options: {"A":"Age of onset under 45 years","B":"Initial presentation with bulbar symptoms","C":"Long duration between first symptom and diagnosis","D":"Male sex","E":"Purely upper motor neurone signs (Primary Lateral Sclerosis phenotype)"}
feedback: Initial presentation with bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia) is associated with a more rapid progression and shorter median survival compared to limb-onset disease. Conversely, younger age of onset, a longer time between symptom onset and diagnosis (suggesting a slower-moving disease process), and the Primary Lateral Sclerosis phenotype (which can have a very slow progression over decades) are generally associated with a better prognosis.

question: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after falling in her kitchen and hitting her head on a cupboards. She did not lose consciousness but reports a mild headache. She has a past medical history of atrial fibrillation for which she takes apixaban. On examination, her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 15/15 and there are no focal neurological deficits. According to NICE guidelines, what is the most appropriate next step in her management?
options: {"A":"Discharge with written head injury advice","B":"Observation in the clinical decision unit for 4 hours","C":"CT head within 1 hour","D":"CT head within 8 hours","E":"Urgent MRI brain"}
feedback: According to NICE guideline CG176/NG232, for patients who have sustained a head injury and are on any anticoagulant (including direct-acting oral anticoagulants like apixaban), a CT head should be performed within 1 hour, regardless of their GCS or the presence of other risk factors. This is due to the high risk of intracranial haemorrhage in anticoagulated patients.

question:
A 34-year-old man is being treated in the Intensive Care Unit four days after suffering a severe traumatic brain injury. The nursing staff report that his urine output has increased significantly to 550 mL/hour over the last three hours. Recent blood and urine results are as follows:

Sodium: 152 mmol/L [135–145 mmol/L]
Potassium: 4.1 mmol/L [3.5–5.0 mmol/L]
Serum Osmolality: 315 mOsm/kg [275–295 mOsm/kg]
Urine Osmolality: 110 mOsm/kg [300–900 mOsm/kg]

What is the most likely complication occurring in this patient?
options: {"A":"Cranial diabetes insipidus","B":"Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)","C":"Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state","D":"Acute kidney injury"}
feedback: Cranial diabetes insipidus (DI) is a common complication of traumatic brain injury due to damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary gland, leading to insufficient ADH production. It is characterised by polyuria, hypernatraemia (Sodium 152), high serum osmolality (315), and inappropriately dilute urine (Urine osmolality 110). SIADH and Cerebral Salt Wasting would both typically present with hyponatraemia.

question: A 20-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedics following a high-speed road traffic accident. On arrival, he is breathing spontaneously but is deeply unconscious. On examination, he opens his eyes only to painful stimuli, makes incomprehensible sounds, and shows an abnormal flexion (decorticate) response to pain. His pupils are equal and reactive. What is the most immediate priority in the management of this patient?
options: {"A":"Urgent CT scan of the head and cervical spine","B":"Intravenous 20% mannitol bolus","C":"Endotracheal intubation and ventilation","D":"Administration of intravenous tranexamic acid","E":"Insertion of an intracranial pressure (ICP) monitor"}
feedback: The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 7 (Eyes: 2, Verbal: 2, Motor: 3). A fundamental rule in emergency medicine for traumatic brain injury is that a patient with a GCS of 8 or less cannot reliably maintain or protect their airway. Therefore, immediate endotracheal intubation and ventilation (the 'A' in ABCDE) is the priority before moving to imaging or specific treatments for intracranial pressure.

question: A 25-year-old man who sustained a severe traumatic brain injury three months ago is being reviewed. He has finished his acute surgical care but remains medically stable with significant impairments, including right-sided hemiparesis, cognitive processing delays, and dysphagia. He requires intensive, coordinated input from physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy to regain independence. Which setting is most appropriate for this phase of his rehabilitation?
options: {"A":"General Practice (GP) community follow-up","B":"Residential nursing home with basic care","C":"Outpatient musculoskeletal physiotherapy clinic","D":"Tertiary neuro-rehabilitation centre","E":"Acute neurosurgical ward"}
feedback: In the post-acute phase of a severe TBI, patients with complex, multi-modal needs (physical, cognitive, and communicative) require a tertiary neuro-rehabilitation centre. These centres provide intensive, specialist multidisciplinary team (MDT) input that is not typically available in general wards or community settings. Community rehab follows this phase once the patient is ready to transition back to home life.

question: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of his right arm and leg. His symptoms began following an ischaemic stroke involving the deep structures of the brain. On examination, the movements are continuous and involuntary, occurring at the proximal joints of the right side. A lesion in which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this hyperkinetic presentation?
options: {"A":"Subthalamic nucleus","B":"Substantia nigra pars compacta","C":"Caudate nucleus","D":"Globus pallidus externus","E":"Putamen"}
feedback: The clinical presentation describes hemiballismus, which is characterized by wild, flinging, proximal limb movements. This typically results from a lesion in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus (STN), often due to a lacunar stroke. The STN is part of the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia; its loss leads to reduced excitation of the globus pallidus internus, resulting in decreased inhibition of the thalamus and subsequent hyperkinesia. Lesions of the striatum (caudate/putamen) more typically cause chorea.

question: A 72-year-old man presents to his GP with a bilateral hand tremor that has worsened over the last five years. He notes that the tremor is most troublesome when he is eating soup or trying to write. He mentions that a small glass of wine in the evening significantly reduces the severity of the shaking. On examination, there is a high-frequency postural tremor when his arms are outstretched, but no resting tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Parkinson’s disease","B":"Essential tremor","C":"Cerebellar tremor","D":"Dystonic tremor","E":"Physiological tremor"}
feedback: Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder. It is typically a postural and kinetic tremor (occurring during action) that is often bilateral and frequently improves with alcohol consumption. It is distinguished from Parkinson’s disease by the absence of resting tremor and other parkinsonian features (bradykinesia, rigidity). Cerebellar tremors are typically intention tremors (worsening as the hand reaches a target) and are often associated with other cerebellar signs like ataxia.

question: A 24-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department with severe nausea and vomiting. She is administered a dose of intravenous prochlorperazine. Thirty minutes later, she develops an acute, sustained involuntary upward deviation of her eyes and her neck becomes painfully twisted to the left side. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's acute symptoms?
options: {"A":"Levodopa","B":"Propranolol","C":"Procyclidine","D":"Tetrabenazine","E":"Botulinum toxin"}
feedback: The patient is experiencing an acute dystonic reaction (specifically an oculogyric crisis and torticollis) as a side effect of prochlorperazine, which is a dopamine (D2) receptor antagonist. This occurs due to a sudden disruption in the balance between dopaminergic and cholinergic activity in the basal ganglia. The management is the administration of an anticholinergic medication, such as procyclidine or benztropine, which rapidly resolves the spasm.

question: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the neurology clinic with a tremor in her right leg. She reports that the tremor started abruptly two weeks ago following a period of significant emotional stress. On examination, when she is asked to perform a complex, rhythmic tapping task with her left hand, the tremor in her right leg is observed to stop or change frequency to match the hand tapping. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {"A":"Dystonic tremor","B":"Functional tremor","C":"Holmes tremor","D":"Myoclonic tremor","E":"Orthostatic tremor"}
feedback: The clinical features described are classic for a functional (psychogenic) movement disorder. Key features include abrupt onset and 'distractibility' or 'entrainment'. Entrainment occurs when the frequency of an involuntary tremor shifts to match the frequency of a voluntary movement performed by another body part. While stressful events can precede functional disorders, the physical sign of entrainment is more diagnostic than the history of stress alone.

question: A 32-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with a long-standing history of progressive loss of pain and temperature sensation across his shoulders and both arms in a 'cape-like' distribution. He recently burned his hand on a kettle without feeling any pain. On examination, his light touch, vibration, and proprioception are preserved in the same distribution. What is the most likely underlying pathology?
options: {"A":"Brown-Séquard syndrome","B":"Syringomyelia","C":"Multiple sclerosis","D":"Anterior cord syndrome","E":"Cervical spondylosis"}
feedback: B is correct because Syringomyelia involves the formation of a fluid-filled cyst (syrinx) within the spinal cord, which typically compresses the decussating fibers of the spinothalamic tract in the anterior white commissure. This leads to a 'dissociated' sensory loss (loss of pain and temperature but preservation of dorsal column modalities like vibration and proprioception) in a cape-like distribution. A is incorrect as Brown-Séquard (hemicord) causes ipsilateral dorsal column loss and contralateral spinothalamic loss. D is incorrect as anterior cord syndrome typically involves motor loss and preserves dorsal columns but would not present in a localized cape distribution. E and C are unlikely to produce this specific pattern of dissociated sensory loss.

question: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of progressive tingling in her feet and hands, followed by ascending weakness. She mentions having a diarrhoeal illness three weeks ago. On examination, she has symmetrical distal sensory loss and global areflexia. Her heart rate is 105 bpm and blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to monitor her immediate clinical risk?
options: {"A":"Arterial blood gas (ABG)","B":"Lumbar puncture","C":"Serial forced vital capacity (FVC) measurements","D":"Nerve conduction studies (NCS)","E":"Continuous cardiac monitoring"}
feedback: C is correct because the patient likely has Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), likely following a Campylobacter jejuni infection. The most critical risk is acute respiratory failure due to neuromuscular weakness. Serial FVC (or vital capacity) measurements are mandatory to monitor for the need for elective intubation. A is incorrect because ABG changes (hypoxia/hypercapnia) are late signs of respiratory failure. B and D help confirm the diagnosis but do not monitor acute risk. E is important due to autonomic instability in GBS, but FVC is the standard for monitoring the immediate threat to life (respiratory arrest).

question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her GP complaining of 'pins and needles' in her right hand that frequently wakes her up at night. She finds that shaking her hand provides some relief. On examination, there is reduced sensation to pinprick over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, and middle fingers. There is also mild wasting of the thenar eminence. Which anatomical structure is responsible for the compression of the affected nerve?
options: {"A":"Flexor retinaculum","B":"Extensor retinaculum","C":"Pronator teres","D":"Guyon's canal","E":"Bicipital aponeurosis"}
feedback: A is correct. The patient presents with classic symptoms of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS), involving the median nerve. The median nerve is compressed as it passes under the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) in the carpal tunnel. D is incorrect as Guyon's canal involves the ulnar nerve at the wrist. C is incorrect as pronator teres syndrome compresses the median nerve at the elbow, usually causing more proximal symptoms and involving the palmar cutaneous branch (which is spared in CTS). B and E are not associated with median nerve compression at the wrist.

question: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with a sudden onset of 'numbness' involving the entire left side of his body, including his face, arm, and leg. On examination, there is a profound loss of all sensory modalities on the left side. There is no associated motor weakness, no cranial nerve palsy, and no visual field defect. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
options: {"A":"Right parietal lobe","B":"Right internal capsule","C":"Right thalamus","D":"Left brainstem","E":"Right pons"}
feedback: C is correct. This is a classic 'pure sensory stroke,' typically caused by a lacunar infarct in the contralateral thalamus (specifically the VPL and VPM nuclei). A pure sensory stroke is characterized by hemi-sensory loss without cortical signs (like aphasia or neglect) or motor deficits. A is incorrect as parietal lobe lesions usually cause 'cortical' sensory loss (loss of two-point discrimination or astereognosis) rather than a global loss of all modalities. B is incorrect as internal capsule lesions usually produce significant motor deficits (pure motor or sensorimotor stroke). D and E are incorrect as brainstem lesions usually produce 'crossed' signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve signs and contralateral body sensory/motor loss).

subtopic: Review of Phase 1 kidney anatomy and renal physiology
question:
A 68-year-old man with long-standing hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes is reviewed in the GP surgery. He has recently started taking Ramipril. A follow-up blood test shows a rise in serum creatinine from 92 µmol/L to 108 µmol/L [Reference range: 60–110 µmol/L]. This rise is attributed to a functional decrease in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

What is the primary physiological mechanism by which this medication reduces GFR?
options: {"A":"Constriction of the afferent arteriole","B":"Dilation of the efferent arteriole","C":"Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter","D":"Stimulation of mesangial cell contraction","E":"Increase in the hydrostatic pressure of the Bowman's space"}
feedback: ACE inhibitors reduce the production of Angiotensin II.
